assessmentSummary.identity: Within the existing two-hand standing rotational-throw definition, the static scoop variant starts side-on with the ball held in two hands low near the back hip, permits a controlled ground-up pivot, and projects to a declared horizontal or slightly rising wall target before a throw-only finish and full reset on each side.
currentCardFindings: Migration 382 already consolidated rotational scoop wording as a release-style variant of the two-hand rotational throw; this batch preserves that stable identity.
The existing canonical card is structurally complete but lacks a selectable exact scoop-release variant with low start position, two-hand sweep, throw-only return policy, and side dosage.
Five oEmbed-healthy rotational-scoop title candidates remain candidate-only and unapproved.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Project a declared medicine ball with two hands from a standing athletic base into an inspected wall using sequenced whole-body rotation. The exact variant states whether the athlete throws and retrieves or tracks, catches, and absorbs a predictable rebound.

population.clinicalBoundary: Symptoms, instability, recent surgery, neurologic signs, or rehabilitation restrictions require individualized clinician guidance; this card is not rehabilitation instruction.
population.selectionBoundary: Select return contract, throw side, ball, target, distance, and dose from current readiness and intended stimulus; exercise cards do not carry proficiency levels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Medicine-ball power assessment depends on a standardized throw task, ball mass, execution, and outcome measure.
Scoop-toss identity must declare forward versus rotational projection, stance and orientation, two-hand release path, ball start position, entry, target, return contract, finish, and side accounting.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Upper-Body Plyometric Training on Physical Fitness in Healthy Youth and Young Adult Participants: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
claims: Medicine-ball throws are ballistic power exercises whose position, direction, release, and outcome must remain controlled taxonomy dimensions.
The forward task is a bilateral sagittal hinge-and-throw; the rotational scoop is a two-hand transverse release variant of the standing rotational-throw definition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Standing medicine-ball performance includes lower-body contribution and whole-body coordination rather than an isolated arm action.
Cards represent the feet, ankles, knees, hips, pelvis, trunk, scapulae, shoulders, elbows, wrists, and hands used by the exact stance and release.

evidence.sourceTitle: Analysis of trunk muscle activity in the side medicine-ball throw
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: A side medicine-ball throw recruits trunk musculature differently from a front-facing throw and requires a side-specific rotational contract.
The forward scoop preserves a front-facing underhand projection; the rotational scoop preserves a side-on hip-to-trunk-to-ball sequence and controlled pivot.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Throw technique and ball mass affect performance variability and task demands.
Difficulty scores exercise complexity and physical difficulty only, with overall derived as their maximum; athlete proficiency is not an exercise-card field.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Medicine-ball mass and throw technique affect measured velocity and performance variability.
Standardize ball and technique when comparing output; operationally track visible output change, volume, rest, symptoms, and recovery without claiming a universal threshold.

evidence.sourceTitle: Land-Based Strength and Conditioning for Swimming
claims: Standing medicine-ball projection requires an intact appropriate ball, stable non-slip surface, inspected target or open lane, and a cleared flight, rebound, and retrieval zone.
Pain, unsafe grip, uncontrolled pivot or finish, uncertain wall or ball behavior, insufficient space, or inability to follow the stop command blocks selection.
High-intent medicine-ball throws use low repetition counts and enough rest to preserve ballistic intent rather than becoming conditioning.
Dose is fully reset throws, counted by side when rotational, with a declared mass, target, return policy, speed-loss rule, and weekly exposure budget.

evidence.sourceTitle: Land-Based Strength and Conditioning for Swimming
claims: Instructions must state stance, ball position, load direction, ground-up sequence, release target, finish, retrieval or return policy, and reset.
Coach observable outcomes such as foot pressure, hip and trunk sequence, release vector, target, balance, and speed rather than promising transfer or injury prevention.

evidence.sourceTitle: Analysis of trunk muscle activity in the side medicine-ball throw
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Rotational throwing creates rapid trunk activity and must stop when the athlete substitutes uncontrolled lumbar motion, loses the pivot, or develops symptoms.
Both tasks stop for pain, grip loss, lane entry, ball or target failure, unsafe flight or rebound, balance loss, target drift, or two consecutive slow or technically changed throws.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: A standardized rotational throw can support power assessment only when protocol and outcome measurement remain stable.

Workout generation must validate exact variant, phase, ball, target, lane, return contract, side balance, duration, rest, cumulative throwing budget, substitutions, and persistence after every change.
Athlete support explains the intended vector, ball and target, what a fast controlled rep looks like, why full rest matters, unexpected symptoms, self-checks, and how to request an alternative.
The athlete never catches, retrieves, steps, jumps, or changes sides unless the selected profile explicitly requires it.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Coaches standardize ball mass, stance, side, target, distance, release vector, measurement method, rest, and valid-attempt rules before comparing outputs.
Group delivery requires a closed flight and retrieval lane, one thrower per zone, shared start and stop signals, side tracking, equipment inspection, and a maintained sightline.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Changing seated versus standing support or forward versus rotational technique changes the task rather than merely changing difficulty.
Accessible delivery may reduce ball mass, effort, repetitions, target precision, or measurement pressure and increase rest or multimodal instruction while preserving the selected identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Analysis of trunk muscle activity in the side medicine-ball throw
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Forward, vertical, reverse-overhead, rotational, chest-pass, and single-arm shot-put releases are separate identities or release families.

Ball mass, target, measured outcome, rest, and modest load depth are modifiers; support position, dynamic entry, jump, catch, and compound follow-up actions require explicit variant or identity review.
